title: Short-Term Incidence of Property Tax Hikes on Professionally Managed Apartments: Evidence from Philadelphia (Ding, Hou & Zhang; Philadelphia Fed WP 26-51; Nov 2026)
what_was_fetched: Fed in Print record (one curl attempt failed with an HTTP/2 INTERNAL_ERROR, no refusal; the record was then read via WebFetch, which gave the abstract and the PDF link). Official PDF https://www.philadelphiafed.org/-/media/frbp/assets/working-papers/2026/wp26-51.pdf (link taken from the Fed in Print record, not guessed) downloaded to dl1/wp26-51.pdf (847 KB, 29 pp.), pdftotext to item1-wp26-51-fulltext.txt. READ IN FULL (text, footnotes, Tables 1-4, figure captions; figure images not inspected).
verdict: NEW research/ding-hou-zhang-philadelphia-property-tax-incidence.md (suggested slug) + ENRICH benefits/landlords-cannot-pass-lvt-to-tenants.md (one sentence) . Clean within-city continuous DiD on a property-level panel; no land/structure split, so it is honest counter-evidence on building-inclusive property tax pass-through, not on LVT. Wire as challenged_by (short-run, professionally managed large apartments), with the land caveat stated on the page.
claim_grade: B. Source tier: Tier 1 (Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, official body; co-author Yilin Hou, Syracuse, recognised public-finance scholar). Preliminary working paper ('circulated for discussion purposes'), not peer reviewed. The 73% headline is a calibrated ratio, not an estimated coefficient (see uncertainties) so grade that figure B- / attribute as the authors' own calculation.

content_summary.event: Philadelphia released new assessments in May 2022 for tax year 2023 (p.3, s2.1 p.5). Philadelphia had no comprehensive reassessment from the 1980s until the Actual Value Initiative (2013); then commercial 2018, residential 2019, all properties 2022 (effective 2023); next in Aug 2024 (fn 10). City-wide residential median assessed value +36.7%, median tax levy +34.4%, mean about +$630 per property (p.3, p.5). Single-family (Table 1): median assessed value $124,600 to $174,200 (+39.8%), median levy $1,667 to $2,307 (+38.4%) vs +3.3% in peer cities. RealPage large apartments (Table 1): median assessed value +7.0%, median levy +0.9% (peer cities +3.9%/+0.5%); 54.7% of RealPage properties saw a tax increase (Fig 2, p.11); wide dispersion because apartments (5+ units) are valued by income or cost approach, and 10-year abatements shield new buildings (s2.1). Single tax rate for all property types, tax is on land plus improvements together.
content_summary.rent_data: RealPage: national panel of professionally managed multifamily properties with 20+ units, monthly asking and effective rent, occupancy, asset grade; 200-plus Philadelphia buildings (221 in the sample; 197 matched to CoreLogic by address, p.10 fn 13), 45,424 units at March 2020 = about 12.5% of the city's rental stock, mean effective rent $1,955 (May 2022); more than 2,800 buildings / 592,795 units in 10 peer cities (Baltimore, Boston, Chicago, Cleveland, Minneapolis, New York, Pittsburgh, Portland OR, Seattle, DC; fn 10). CoreLogic for assessments, tax amounts. Zillow ZORI (zip-level asking-rent index, whole market) for market-level test. Period 2020 to Q1 2024; unbalanced panel (fn 16).
content_summary.design: Two designs. (1) Continuous DiD within Philadelphia RealPage properties: treatment = property's own 2022-to-2023 tax change per $100 of assessed value, interacted with quarter dummies, baseline 2022Q2, property controls and zip effects, unit-weighted (eq 1, s3.1; Table 3). The 'control' is low-tax-change Philadelphia buildings, not peer cities. No pre-trend (Fig 3, Table 3). (2) Standard DiD, Philadelphia vs 10 peer cities (RealPage and ZORI), plus synthetic DiD (eq 2; Fig 4, Table 4, Figs A1-A2); this one has a pre-trend in 2020 Q1-Q2 (Philadelphia rents 5-6% lower), SDiD gives -0.7% to -0.4%, insignificant.
content_summary.pass_through_73: Exact wording, abstract p.1: 'We document that about 73 percent of tax increases were passed through to tenants in professionally managed large-scale apartments, with effects emerging approximately three quarters after the policy shock.' Derivation, s4.2 pp.12-13: 'for apartment buildings that had a $1 property tax increase per $100 of assessed value, their effective and asking rents would increase by 8.7% to 9.0% within one-and-a-half years' (Fig 3; March 2024 estimates 8.7% effective, 9.0% asking). Then: 'an average RealPage property ... assessed at approximately $280,000 per unit ... A $1 increase in the tax rate (per $100 assessed value) translates to an annual tax increase of approximately $2,800 per unit, while an 8.7% rent increase amounts to $2,041 annually (or 73% of the annual tax increase of $2,800)'. Fn 15: the $280,000 rests on a 5% cap rate and 40% expense ratio and a $220,000-$335,000 purchase-cost range from Northmarq. The Introduction (p.3) says 'a pass-through rate of almost 75%', abstract/body say 73%. Table 3 average post-period effects (standard continuous DiD): ln asking rent 0.051 (SE 0.010), ln effective rent 0.033 (SE 0.010), p<0.001/0.001.
content_summary.timing: Interaction coefficients turn positive and significant at 0.001 from 2023Q1, 'three quarters after the announcement of new assessments' (p.12); explained by lease cycles and the lag from assessment (May 2022) to bill (late 2022) to payment (early 2023) (p.13). (Fed in Print abstract renders this as 'nine months'.)
content_summary.market_level: No significant effect: RealPage Philadelphia vs peer cities, none of the interaction coefficients significant though positive for asking rent (p.13-14); ZORI Philadelphia-vs-peers coefficient negative and insignificant, log -0.035 (SE 0.016, p=0.052), level -$161.6 (p=0.098) (Table 4). ZORI rose 6.5% (May 2022 to Mar 2024) in Philadelphia vs 8.9% average in peer cities (p.11). Authors' reconciliation: only slightly over half of large multifamily properties saw increases, mostly small; smaller multifamily and single-family rentals likely pass through less 'although we cannot test the second factor directly owing to data limitations'; DiD 'missing intercept' caveat (Watson & Ziv 2025).
content_summary.heterogeneity: Theory framing from Weyl & Fabinger (2013) on pass-through under imperfect competition and from algorithmic-pricing literature (Calder-Wang & Kim 2024). There is NO measured market-concentration or market-structure variable in the paper; the only heterogeneity is professionally managed large buildings (continuous DiD) vs everything else seen through ZORI. The 'larger, sophisticated landlords pass through faster' reading is the authors' interpretation, flagged as indirect (s2.2, s4.2 'Summary').
content_summary.land_vs_structure: Nothing. The tax is on assessed land plus improvements; fn 1 restricts the study to residential real estate tax; abatement exempts improvement value on new construction but there is no land/improvement decomposition and no LVT discussion.
content_summary.long_run: Explicitly short-term (about two years). Authors: 'it is still too early to observe the full effects'; landlords 'may also resort to other means to shift the costs on to tenants in the long term'; long-term incidence flagged as future research (p.4, p.15-17). Literature table in s2.2: pass-through 15% (Carroll & Yinger 1994) to 40-50% in recent studies, almost 100% for commercial (Rolheiser 2019), 50-89% for new renters in Berkeley (Baker 2025, Phil. Fed WP 25-41); ITEP uses 50% (Davis et al. 2024).

existing_wiki_coverage: Read: research/loffler-siegloch-german-pass-through.md (full pass-through in Germany within about 3 years, land-plus-improvements base, lower where supply inelastic), research/carroll-yinger-benefit-tax-rental.md (about $0.15 per $1), research/schwegman-yinger-homestead.md (about 14%), research/tsoodle-turner-rents.md (rents rise $400-450 per SD of rate), research/hilber-capitalization-synthesis.md (exists), concepts/tax-capitalization.md, benefits/landlords-cannot-pass-lvt-to-tenants.md (hub; 'Evidence' section and 'Strength of Evidence' bullets already carry the short-run-frictions caveat), research/mieszkowski-property-tax-incidence.md, research/zodrow-three-views.md. No page for Baker (2025) Philadelphia Fed WP 25-41 (grep: none) or for Ding/Hou/Zhang. No standalone objection page on 'LVT passed on to tenants'; the benefits hub is the carrier. ENRICH ANCHOR (benefits/landlords-cannot-pass-lvt-to-tenants.md, 'Evidence', paragraph 'Rental markets'), exact text: '[Löffler & Siegloch](/wiki/loffler-siegloch-german-pass-through/), exploiting ~5,200\nGerman municipal reforms, find **full pass-through to rents within three years**.' Proposed addition after it: 'A 2026 Philadelphia Fed working paper exploiting the city's delayed 2023 reassessment finds that landlords of professionally managed large apartments passed through about 73 percent of tax increases within about three quarters, while citywide rents showed no significant change ([Ding, Hou & Zhang](/wiki/ding-hou-zhang-philadelphia-property-tax-incidence/)).' Alternative anchor in the 'Strength of Evidence' bullet 'Property-tax pass-through is institution-dependent and genuinely disputed': '(Orr 1968; Carroll & Yinger; Schwegman & Yinger) against real pass-through in\n  others ([Tsoodle & Turner](/wiki/tsoodle-turner-rents/); Heinberg & Oates 1970;'. Also add a See Also line on research/loffler-siegloch-german-pass-through.md and research/tsoodle-turner-rents.md.
uncertainties: SCANNER PREMISES: (a) 'delayed comprehensive reassessment' correct; (b) '73%' is correct but it is a back-of-envelope ratio computed from an 8.7% rent coefficient and an assumed $280,000 assessed value per unit, not an estimated pass-through parameter; the intro says 'almost 75%'; (c) 'about 3 quarters' correct; (d) 'no significant market-level rent increase' correct; (e) the scanner's 'serves hilber-capitalization-synthesis, loffler-siegloch, han-ngai-sheedy' is a loose fit: the paper has no land/structure or tenure analysis.

Internal tension worth a caution on the page: Table 1 gives a median RealPage-property assessed value of $17.3M (2022) and Table 2 gives 45,424 units over about 221 properties (about 205 units per property), implying roughly $85k assessed per unit, far below the $280k used in the 73% calculation (fn 15 builds it from a cap-rate and purchase-price assumption, not from assessments; median vs mean and abatements may explain part of the gap). If the assessed value per unit were lower, the implied dollar tax change per unit would be lower and the ratio higher. Say only that the 73% rests on the authors' stated assumption.

A web-search snippet (not read in full) shows a 2025 conference version (NTA) of apparently the same study titled 'Who Really Pays: the Short-term Incidence of the Property Tax in Philadelphia' concluding that landlords bear the burden with no rent response after about two years; the conclusion changed between versions (identity of the two papers not confirmed). Do not cite the conference abstract.
Fed in Print abstract says 'roughly nine months'; the PDF says 'approximately three quarters'; same thing.
Figures (event-study charts) were not viewed; numbers above come from text and tables only.
Baker (2025) is a separate, relevant Fed working paper (50-89% pass-through to new renters in Berkeley, quasi-random building-level shocks); not read here; candidate for its own queue item.

Is a NEW page warranted? Yes: modern US quasi-experimental rental-incidence evidence from an official source, adjacent to the Schwegman-Yinger and Löffler-Siegloch pages, with a result that cuts against the hub claim in the short run.

content_summary.abstract_verbatim: 'Informal settlements are often portrayed as marginal spaces, excluded from formal economies and property regimes - a framing that obscures the social differentiation within them. This article examines how the landlord-tenant hierarchy structures inequality in Zandspruit, an informal settlement on the periphery of Johannesburg. Drawing on over a decade of ethnographic research, it shows how land and housing operate as income-generating assets, producing a divide between landlords - typically long-standing residents who lease backyard rooms or subdivided plots - and tenants - often newer arrivals or migrants reliant on insecure wage work and rental housing. Situated within South Africa's history of racialized dispossession and post-apartheid labour-market precarity, the article brings theories of rentier capitalism into dialogue with anthropological work on distribution. It shows how grassroots rentierism, grounded in popular notions of ownership and legitimacy rather than formal title, involve intra-local distribution and extraction that intensify inequalities within marginalized urban communities. The article demonstrates how class differentiation is reproduced through rent extraction within local distributional circuits, rather than solely through employment.' (Crossref abstract and UJ portal, identical.)
content_summary.confirmed_from_abstract: Setting Zandspruit, informal settlement on Johannesburg's periphery; fieldwork 'over a decade' of ethnography; landlords = long-standing residents leasing backyard rooms or subdivided plots; tenants = newer arrivals or migrants in insecure wage work; the concept 'grassroots rentierism' grounded in popular notions of ownership and legitimacy rather than formal title; engagement with 'theories of rentier capitalism' and anthropology of distribution. 86 references (Crossref) so the engagement is substantial.
content_summary.not_available: Fieldwork years, rents, share of households renting, number of backyard rooms, and whether Christophers or Standing are the rentier-capitalism authors engaged: none in the abstract; not verified.

Proposed addition as a new short subsection after it (or after Bartilow, before '## The Contested Boundary of "Rent"'): '### Dawson: Grassroots Rentierism in an Informal Settlement -- A 2026 Development and Change article by Hannah J. Dawson, drawing on more than a decade of ethnographic research in Zandspruit, an informal settlement on the periphery of Johannesburg, describes a landlord-tenant divide in which long-standing residents who lease backyard rooms or subdivided plots extract rent from newer arrivals and migrants, a "grassroots rentierism, grounded in popular notions of ownership and legitimacy rather than formal title" that she argues reproduces class differentiation through rent extraction rather than employment alone.[n]' Source line: Dawson (2026), Development and Change 57(4): 680-705, doi:10.1111/dech.70055 -- 'abstract read via Crossref and the University of Johannesburg research portal; full text not read' (impersonal Sources-only wording; no process narration in the body).

Open access is real (Crossref licence and Unpaywall both say CC BY-NC-ND hybrid OA) but Wiley refused the one ordinary request with a bot challenge; per policy not retried. A reader with a browser could fetch the OA PDF; T0 cannot.
